text: Lesson one defined trust concretely: every customer has a non-null customer ID, and every customer ID is unique. This lesson is where that definition stops being a sentence and becomes something dbt actually checks, every time the project runs.

Here's the real file, living right next to the staging model: stg_jaffle_shop__customers dot yml. Version 2, a models block naming stg_jaffle_shop__customers, and under its customer_id column, a data_tests key listing not_null and unique. Same syntax, same two generic tests from the prerequisite dbt course — just written against this project's own primary key.

not_null checks that customer_id is never blank — it compiles to roughly a select where customer_id is null, and any returned rows mean a failure. unique checks that no customer_id value ever repeats. Both tests are really just select statements that should return zero rows — the exact mental model the dbt course already taught, now applied for real.
Run them with dbt test, select stg_jaffle_shop__customers. A clean run reports PASS for both — one of two, PASS, not null on customer_id, two of two, PASS, unique on customer_id.

If the real data had a blank or duplicate customer ID, this same run would show a FAIL line instead — one duplicate found, for example. The honest move isn't deleting the test. It's querying the staging model directly, finding the actual failing row, and figuring out why the raw data has a duplicate — the same troubleshooting habit from the dbt course's testing chapter.

This is the literal, checkable answer to the Ops Manager's ask from Lesson 1 — not a feeling, a passing test anyone can run. Next lesson, we build on top of this trusted staging model — the customer mart, the final table finance and support will actually query, using ref() instead of source() for the first time in this project.
